newsitem.title: USA: Study links abortion, breast cancer.
newsitem.headline: Study links abortion, breast cancer.

text.p: Having an abortion increases a woman's risk of developing breast cancer by one third, according to a study released on Friday based on previous research on the issue.

The study, a statistical analysis of 23 earlier studies of a total of nearly 26,000 women with breast cancer and nearly 35,000 cancer-free women, was in the October issue of the Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health, published by the British Medical Association.
It was written by researchers from Penn State University's Hershey Medical Centre in Hershey, Pennsylvania, and Baruch College in New York City.

The article said there was no consensus in the medical community regarding a link between breast cancer and abortion and the community had played down evidence supporting such a risk. But the results demonstrated that women considering abortions should be warned that a greater risk of breast cancer existed, it said.
Other medical authorities believe the evidence of a connection remains too weak to justify, for example, legislation mandating warnings to women considering abortions.

"The potential of induced abortions as a breast cancer risk factor continues largely to be minimised," the article said. "While the need for further research cannot be denied ... there exists the more present need for those in clinical practice to inform their patients fully about what is already known."

In a news release, the study's authors estimated that abortions now accounted for about 5,000 cases of breast cancer in the United States every year and that number could reach 25,000 by the middle of the next century. In comparison, women who suffered early miscarriages did not experience a similar risk, the authors said.

They said the trigger for the increased risk was the build-up of oestrogen during pregnancy. In women who carried pregnancies to term, hormones secreted near the end of the pregnancy modified the growth and vulnerability of breast cells and resulted in a lower cancer risk, they said.
Many spontaneous abortions -- miscarriages -- occur very early in pregnancy before oestrogen levels rise sharply, they said.
"Excess exposure to oestrogen is involved in most known breast cancer risk factors," said Joel Brind, a professor of endocrinology at Baruch College and one of the study's four authors.

In January, a study of 16,000 American women published in the Journal of the American Medical Association showed women who had either a miscarriage or an abortion had a 12 percent higher risk of breast cancer than women who have never terminated a pregnancy. The risk was unrelated to whether the abortion was spontanteous or induced.

The Journal said in an editorial at the time that studies on the issue conflicted and that proposed legislation in several states to require that women be warned of potential risks of abortion was premature.
